questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was crucial to me that the study destination was a german speaking country

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university was good at keeping students informed about all the practical matters that needed to be sorted out before and after arrival. They held several online meetings where they explained various things and matters.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Once again, they were excellent at providing information – for example, that you had to register at the Bürgeramt, where you could collect your student ID card, and so on. However, there were also many things they didn’t mention, which you had to sort out yourself. For example, the VPN for the university’s website (IT support weren’t very helpful).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Generally speaking, you should expect to take the initiative yourself, get in touch with the people who can help you with administrative matters, and keep an eye on deadlines and so on.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It was possible to request a specific price range (there were three in total), but you weren’t guaranteed to get what you wanted. However, I would say that, as a Danish student, the prices of the flats available through the University of Heidelberg were very affordable. You couldn’t choose where in the city you would live, or with whom.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I lived in a flat with two other people; we each had our own room but shared the toilet and kitchen. It was all very sparsely furnished, so you had to go out and buy a lot of things yourself. These included a duvet, pillow, plates, pots and pans, etc. In some places, however, it was possible to borrow things from those who were already living there or to take some of the items left behind by previous flatmates.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: As I said, you don’t get to choose who you live with, and there’s generally a high turnover of tenants in the flats, as many exchange students live there. As a result, hygiene standards aren’t great. Many of the flats are dirty and unsanitary, especially compared to Danish standards. You’re also responsible for drawing up a cleaning rota yourself, so if you end up with flatmates who don’t know how to clean or can’t be bothered to clean, there’s not much you can do about the situation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I suppose I would have found somewhere private to live, rather than through the university

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As the German academic term is so out of sync with everyone else’s, their courses do not become fully available until very late. This clashes significantly with OLA and the pre-approval process

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: During this process, there wasn’t much help to be had from the university. You had to write to each lecturer individually and ask if there was a place on their course. However, they were often very kind in agreeing to accept exchange students

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Non – you just had to hope your teacher would be helpful

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to enrol on all the courses I wanted and received ECTS credits for the ones I wanted. The German system is actually very flexible. You can therefore ask your lecturer whether you can get more ECTS credits for a module than are actually allocated.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The whole process of choosing modules happens quite late compared to what we’re used to. I didn’t finalise my module choices until the first week of term. Find some modules you find interesting, give them a go for the first week or so, and then decide which ones you want to sit the exams in. The lecturers don’t ask who’s sitting the exams until the end of the semester, so you’ve plenty of time to work out which modules you’d like to sit the exams in.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were lots of interesting subjects, which were also much more specialised

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: In Germany, they don’t divide courses into BA and MA, at least not in the humanities, so most subjects were open to students to take

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lecturers have a fair amount of autonomy over their own courses. They can choose the syllabus themselves, how many ECTS credits you receive for the course, and so on.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There was a student fee of 80 euros, and then there was the fact that you had to buy lots of things for your flat

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport is very expensive in Germany, but it’s easy to cycle around Heidelberg, so that’s what I did instead, which is why it didn’t end up being that expensive after all

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The town is incredibly charming and filled with young people

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university offered sports activities which were brilliant and very cheap

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Take up a sport. I used to do Pilates myself, but I also know several people who joined a running club

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Take up a sport. I used to do Pilates myself, but I also know several people who joined a running club. What’s more, there are some great swimming pools and cinemas in the town

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: There isn’t much difference between Denmark and Germany, so it went really well.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: You could try taking up a sport or enrol on a German course where there are other students learning German. I got to know people through group work, for example.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Germans can be very strict about rules and aren’t always particularly helpful. When you have to deal with the authorities or other administrative matters, it can sometimes be quite a hassle.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They are much more keen to preserve old traditions, language and culture. It’s far cooler to be a humanities student in Germany than in Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be prepared for things to be a bit of a faff at times when you’re coordinating with two universities, but it’ll all work out in the end. 
It’s hard to make friends with the locals in just half a year, but there are plenty of lovely exchange students in Heidelberg too. 
Go and explore whilst you’re in Central Europe. Everything’s much closer by

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think i covered it all

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To improve my German

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It’s probably down to my living situation, but mostly because of my flatmates

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Be aware of the summer heat in Heidelberg!!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
